CHIEF COMPLAINT
Second opinion regarding right index finger injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male presenting for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. He sustained a hyperextension injury to the right index finger during a motor vehicle accident in March 2026 when the vehicle was rear-ended multiple times, causing him to be thrust forward and stretch out his right index finger. He reports the finger has been painful and swollen since the accident, approximately three months ago. He cannot make a fist and describes the pain as sometimes unbearable, exacerbated by activities such as driving. He was seen at Point May Orthopedics by physical therapy and PA staff and underwent an MRI on 4/24/2026 that revealed partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon, fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDS and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendons, and focal soft tissue swelling over the right index metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. The patient reports receiving conflicting information regarding treatment recommendations and feeling he is not receiving adequate medical care. He is right-handed and requires use of this hand for his occupation as an X-ray technician.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. No other systemic complaints documented.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
History of reaction to dexamethasone (causes tachycardia). History of itching with methylprednisolone.

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication.

ALLERGIES
Adverse reaction to dexamethasone (tachycardia). Adverse reaction to methylprednisolone (pruritus).

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as an X-ray technician. Right-handed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no acute distress. Vitals: Heart rate regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulse bilaterally. Hand/Finger: No swelling or bruising in palm over volar surface of index finger. Normal creases slightly diminished over proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of index finger compared to middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Patient reports pain with passive correction and tenderness to palpation. Mild numbness noted. Active range of motion testing demonstrates pain with flexion and extension. MCP joint pain elicited with flexion testing. Right hand X-rays (four views) today: No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.

RESULTS
MRI of right index finger (4/24/2026): Focal soft tissue swelling over right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of right FDS tendon, fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around FDP and FDS tendons, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of index MCP joint intact, MCP joint capsule intact, extensor tendons intact. X-rays right hand today: No bony abnormalities, normal joint congruency, no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of right index finger with partial-thickness tear of flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. The patient has significant scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon blocking excursion of other tendons. Plan: (1) Steroid injection today using 1 cc betamethasone (Celestone) with 0.5 cc lidocaine to avoid dexamethasone and methylprednisolone due to documented adverse reactions. Note: Patient had dramatic and violent painful reaction to initial needle insertion with hand withdrawal and concerns for needle stick. Injection was completed on second attempt with small palmar vein bleeding managed with band-aid. Patient counseled on importance of steroid injection and reassured regarding safety. (2) Ice and ibuprofen as needed this evening. (3) Aggressive range of motion exercises—patient instructed that splinting immobilizes rather than helps and that active movement is critical for recovery. (4) Outpatient occupational therapy once weekly for six weeks with goal of full active and passive range of motion without restrictions. Patient encouraged to resume therapy at Point May Orthopedics where he was previously treated, with expectation that improved pain control from injection will allow better participation. Reassured that collateral ligaments and extensors are intact, so aggressive motion will not cause further injury. Advised that pain should improve within 3-5 days and further improve over subsequent weeks. Noted that repeat injection may be needed. Advised that driving is safe despite discomfort.
